sections.title: Title Page
sections.contentHtml:
Clinical Study Report. Protocol VELORA-301. A Phase 3, Randomised, Double-Blind, Multicentre Trial of Veloricept (anti-VEGFR2/anti-PD-L1 bispecific) in combination with Pembrolizumab versus Pembrolizumab plus Platinum-Doublet Chemotherapy in Participants with Previously Untreated, Metastatic Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC) with PD-L1 TPS ≥50%.

Report Version 0.4. Data cutoff: 30 September 2024. Sponsor: GenBioCa Oncology, Inc. Date of this report: 22 October 2024. Report prepared in accordance with ICH E3.

sections.title: Synopsis
sections.contentHtml:
Objective. To evaluate the efficacy and safety of veloricept + pembrolizumab versus pembrolizumab + platinum-doublet chemotherapy as first-line therapy in metastatic NSCLC with PD-L1 TPS ≥50%.

Methods. Phase 3, randomised (1:1), double-blind, multicentre trial. 612 participants were randomised across 94 sites in the US, EU and Japan.

Primary results. At the pre-planned interim analysis (data cutoff 30 September 2024), median progression-free survival (PFS) was 11.8 months (95% CI 9.6–14.1) in the veloricept + pembrolizumab arm versus 7.4 months (95% CI 6.2–8.9) in the comparator arm; hazard ratio 0.62 (95% CI 0.50–0.78; stratified log-rank p<0.0001). Overall survival data remain immature (154 events of 410 required for the final OS analysis).

Conclusions. Veloricept + pembrolizumab produced a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in PFS with a manageable safety profile consistent with the known profiles of each agent.

sections.title: Ethics
sections.contentHtml:
The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki (2013), ICH E6(R3) Good Clinical Practice, applicable national regulations (US: 21 CFR Parts 50, 54, 56, and 312; EU: Clinical Trials Regulation (EU) 536/2014; Japan: PMDA Ordinance on GCP), and the study protocol as amended through Amendment 1 (dated 15 January 2024).

Independent ethics committee (IEC) or institutional review board (IRB) approval was obtained at every investigational site before enrolment commenced. Written informed consent was obtained from each participant on an IRB/IEC-approved consent form (ICF v2) in the local language. No protocol deviations with material impact on participant rights or safety were identified during the reporting period.

sections.title: Investigators & Sites
sections.contentHtml:
The study was conducted at 94 investigational sites across 11 countries: 36 US sites, 28 sites in 7 EU member states, 14 UK sites, 12 Japanese sites, and 4 Canadian sites. The coordinating principal investigator was Prof. Elena Vázquez (Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center). A full listing of investigators, sub-investigators, and site addresses is provided in Appendix 16.1.4.

The Independent Data Monitoring Committee (IDMC) comprised three thoracic oncologists, one biostatistician, and one pharmacovigilance physician. The IDMC convened at four pre-specified safety reviews (after 100, 200, 300, and 450 participants had completed Cycle 4) and recommended continuation without modification on each occasion.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.contentHtml:
Non-small cell lung cancer accounts for approximately 85% of all lung cancer diagnoses and remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. For patients with metastatic NSCLC and high PD-L1 expression (TPS ≥50%), pembrolizumab monotherapy is a standard of care based on the KEYNOTE-024 trial (Reck 2016), with median PFS of approximately 10.3 months.

Veloricept is a first-in-class bispecific antibody targeting VEGFR2 and PD-L1, designed to simultaneously block tumour angiogenesis and restore anti-tumour T-cell immunity in the tumour microenvironment. Phase 1b/2 data (VELORA-101, Chen 2023) demonstrated an ORR of 54% and an acceptable safety profile when combined with pembrolizumab, supporting the Phase 3 investigation reported here.

sections.title: Study Objectives
sections.contentHtml:
Primary objective. To compare progression-free survival (PFS) by blinded independent central review (BICR) per RECIST v1.1 between veloricept + pembrolizumab and pembrolizumab + platinum-doublet chemotherapy.

Key secondary objectives. (i) Overall survival (OS); (ii) objective response rate (ORR) per RECIST v1.1 by BICR; (iii) duration of response (DOR); (iv) safety and tolerability per CTCAE v5.0; (v) health-related quality of life per EORTC QLQ-C30 and QLQ-LC13.

Exploratory objectives included evaluation of PD-L1 TPS subgroups, tumour mutational burden, and circulating tumour DNA dynamics as potential predictive biomarkers.

sections.title: Investigational Plan
sections.contentHtml:
Participants were randomised 1:1 to receive either (Arm A) veloricept 15 mg/kg IV every 3 weeks + pembrolizumab 200 mg IV every 3 weeks, or (Arm B) pembrolizumab 200 mg IV every 3 weeks + investigator's choice of platinum-doublet chemotherapy (carboplatin + pemetrexed for non-squamous; carboplatin + paclitaxel for squamous) for 4 cycles followed by maintenance pembrolizumab (± pemetrexed).

Randomisation was stratified by (a) ECOG performance status (0 vs 1), (b) histology (squamous vs non-squamous), and (c) geographic region (US vs EU vs Japan). Treatment continued until confirmed radiographic progression per RECIST v1.1, unacceptable toxicity, withdrawal of consent, or a maximum of 35 cycles. Tumour imaging was performed every 6 weeks for the first 48 weeks and every 9 weeks thereafter.

sections.title: Efficacy Evaluation
sections.contentHtml:
Efficacy analyses were performed on the ITT population (all randomised participants). The primary endpoint (PFS by BICR per RECIST v1.1) was analysed using a stratified log-rank test. Secondary endpoints were tested in a hierarchical manner to control type I error.

At the data cutoff of 30 September 2024, 342 PFS events had occurred (156 Arm A, 186 Arm B). Median PFS was 11.8 months (95% CI 9.6–14.1) in Arm A versus 7.4 months (95% CI 6.2–8.9) in Arm B; HR 0.62 (95% CI 0.50–0.78), stratified log-rank p<0.0001. The treatment effect was consistent across all pre-specified subgroups.

Confirmed ORR was 61.2% (189/309; 95% CI 55.5–66.6) in Arm A versus 46.5% (141/303; 95% CI 40.8–52.3) in Arm B; odds ratio 1.81 (p=0.0003). Median DOR in responders was not reached in Arm A versus 9.6 months in Arm B.

sections.title: Primary Efficacy Analysis
sections.contentHtml:
The primary efficacy analysis was pre-specified in the Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP v2.0, finalised 15 August 2024, locked prior to database lock on 10 October 2024). The protocol required 320 PFS events for the primary analysis at a two-sided alpha of 0.025 (interim) and 0.025 (final), controlled using an O'Brien-Fleming boundary; the observed 342 events at interim exceeded the threshold and the pre-specified efficacy boundary was crossed.

The hazard ratio was estimated using a stratified Cox proportional hazards model with the three randomisation stratification factors (ECOG PS, histology, region). The proportional hazards assumption was formally tested using Schoenfeld residuals (global p=0.21) and visually by log-cumulative-hazard plots; no violations were identified.

Sensitivity analyses using investigator-assessed PFS (HR 0.65; 95% CI 0.52–0.80) and per-protocol population (HR 0.60; 95% CI 0.48–0.76) were consistent with the primary analysis.

sections.title: Safety Evaluation
sections.contentHtml:
Safety was assessed in all participants who received at least one dose of study treatment (safety population: 303 Arm A, 291 Arm B). Adverse events were coded to MedDRA v27.0 and graded per CTCAE v5.0.

Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) of any grade occurred in 98.0% of Arm A and 99.0% of Arm B. Grade ≥3 TEAEs were reported in 56.8% (172/303) of Arm A and 68.4% (199/291) of Arm B. Treatment-related Grade ≥3 events occurred in 42.6% vs 54.6%, respectively.

sections.title: Discussion & Conclusions
sections.contentHtml:
At the pre-planned interim analysis (data cutoff 30 September 2024), VELORA-301 met its primary endpoint: veloricept + pembrolizumab produced a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in PFS over pembrolizumab + platinum-doublet chemotherapy in first-line metastatic NSCLC with PD-L1 TPS ≥50% (HR 0.62; 95% CI 0.50–0.78; p<0.0001). The ORR advantage (61.2% vs 46.5%) and the depth of response (median DOR not reached vs 9.6 months) support the magnitude of benefit.

The safety profile was manageable and consistent with the known profiles of each agent. VEGF-pathway toxicities (hypertension, proteinuria) were increased with veloricept but rarely led to permanent discontinuation. Immune-related pneumonitis occurred at a slightly higher rate than historical pembrolizumab monotherapy, consistent with the added PD-L1 arm of the bispecific; the rate of Grade 3+ pneumonitis (3.0%) is comparable to contemporary PD-1/PD-L1 combinations.

Overall survival data remain immature; the pre-specified final OS analysis is expected in Q4 2026. The results reported here provide sufficient evidence to support regulatory submissions under accelerated-approval and conditional-approval pathways.

sections.title: Study Centre(s)
sections.contentHtml: Ninety-four (94) investigational sites across 11 countries: United States (36 sites), European Union (28 sites across Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Netherlands, Belgium, Poland), United Kingdom (14 sites), Japan (12 sites), and Canada (4 sites). The lead coordinating site was Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (New York, USA).

sections.title: Phase of Development
sections.contentHtml: Phase 3, pivotal registration trial supporting first-line marketing authorisation applications in the US (BLA), EU (MAA under EMA centralised procedure), and Japan (J-NDA via PMDA).

sections.title: Objectives
sections.contentHtml:
Primary. Compare PFS by BICR per RECIST v1.1 between veloricept + pembrolizumab vs pembrolizumab + platinum-doublet.

Key secondary. OS; ORR; DOR; safety per CTCAE v5.0; patient-reported outcomes (EORTC QLQ-C30, QLQ-LC13); pharmacokinetics; immunogenicity (anti-drug antibodies to veloricept).

sections.title: Methodology / Study Design
sections.contentHtml: Randomised (1:1), double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled, parallel-group, multicentre Phase 3 trial. Randomisation stratified by ECOG PS (0 vs 1), histology (squamous vs non-squamous), and region (US vs EU vs Japan). Treatment continued until confirmed radiographic progression, unacceptable toxicity, consent withdrawal, or 35 cycles (whichever occurred first). Tumour imaging every 6 weeks for the first 48 weeks, then every 9 weeks.

sections.title: Number of Subjects (Planned & Analysed)
sections.contentHtml: Planned: 600 participants (300 per arm). Analysed: 612 randomised (309 Arm A — veloricept + pembrolizumab; 303 Arm B — pembrolizumab + platinum-doublet). Safety population: 594 (303 Arm A, 291 Arm B). 18 participants (6 A, 12 B) did not receive study drug.

sections.title: Diagnosis & Main Criteria for Inclusion
sections.contentHtml: Histologically or cytologically confirmed Stage IV NSCLC with no prior systemic therapy for metastatic disease, PD-L1 TPS ≥50% by central testing (Dako 22C3 pharmDx), ECOG PS 0–1, measurable disease per RECIST v1.1, and life expectancy ≥12 weeks. Participants with sensitising EGFR mutations or ALK/ROS1 rearrangements were excluded.

sections.title: Test Product, Dose & Mode of Administration
sections.contentHtml: Veloricept, a humanised bispecific IgG1 monoclonal antibody targeting VEGFR2 and PD-L1, administered at 15 mg/kg by intravenous infusion over 60 minutes on Day 1 of each 3-week cycle, in combination with pembrolizumab 200 mg IV over 30 minutes on Day 1 of each 3-week cycle.

sections.title: Duration of Treatment
sections.contentHtml: Up to 35 cycles (approximately 24 months) or until confirmed disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, or participant withdrawal. Median duration of exposure at data cutoff: 10.8 cycles in Arm A, 7.4 cycles in Arm B.

sections.title: Reference Therapy
sections.contentHtml: Pembrolizumab 200 mg IV every 3 weeks + investigator's choice of platinum-doublet chemotherapy: carboplatin AUC 5 + pemetrexed 500 mg/m² (non-squamous) OR carboplatin AUC 6 + paclitaxel 200 mg/m² (squamous) for 4 cycles, followed by maintenance pembrolizumab ± pemetrexed. This reflects the standard of care established by KEYNOTE-189 and KEYNOTE-407.

sections.title: Criteria for Evaluation (Efficacy / Safety)
sections.contentHtml:
Efficacy. PFS and ORR by BICR per RECIST v1.1; OS from randomisation to death from any cause; DOR in confirmed responders. Imaging reviewed by two independent radiologists blinded to treatment, with adjudication by a third radiologist for discordant reads.

Safety. Adverse events coded to MedDRA v27.0 and graded per CTCAE v5.0; laboratory assessments; vital signs; ECG; immunogenicity (ADA against veloricept) at pre-specified timepoints.

sections.title: Statistical Methods
sections.contentHtml: Primary analysis: stratified log-rank test on PFS in the ITT population, two-sided alpha allocated 0.025 (interim) / 0.025 (final) with O'Brien-Fleming boundaries. Hazard ratios estimated via stratified Cox proportional hazards model. OS tested in a hierarchical sequence to control type I error. ORR compared using stratified Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test. Pre-specified subgroup analyses by age, sex, race, ECOG PS, histology, PD-L1 subgroup, smoking status, and region.

sections.title: Summary of Efficacy Results
sections.contentHtml: Median PFS 11.8 months (Arm A) vs 7.4 months (Arm B); HR 0.62 (95% CI 0.50–0.78); stratified log-rank p<0.0001. Confirmed ORR 61.2% vs 46.5% (odds ratio 1.81; p=0.0003). Median DOR not reached vs 9.6 months. OS data immature (154 events; 25.2% maturity); interim HR 0.78 (95% CI 0.56–1.08), not formally tested at this analysis.

sections.title: Summary of Safety Results
sections.contentHtml: Grade ≥3 TEAEs: 56.8% (Arm A) vs 68.4% (Arm B). Treatment discontinuation due to AE: 14.9% vs 17.5%. Deaths attributed to AE: 4.0% vs 3.1%. Veloricept-specific AEs of interest included hypertension (Grade ≥3 5.9%), proteinuria (any grade 13.9%), and immune-related pneumonitis (Grade ≥3 3.0%). No new safety signals were identified beyond the known profiles of each agent.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.contentHtml: Veloricept + pembrolizumab demonstrated a statistically significant and clinically meaningful PFS benefit over pembrolizumab + platinum-doublet chemotherapy in first-line metastatic NSCLC with PD-L1 TPS ≥50%, with a manageable safety profile. These results support regulatory submission to the US FDA, EMA, and PMDA.

sections.title: Protocol Synopsis
sections.contentHtml:
VELORA-301 is a Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, multicentre study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of veloricept 15 mg/kg + pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks versus pembrolizumab + platinum-doublet chemotherapy in approximately 600 participants with previously untreated, metastatic NSCLC and PD-L1 TPS ≥50%.

The primary endpoint is PFS by BICR per RECIST v1.1. Key secondary endpoints are OS, ORR, DOR, and safety. The trial is designed to support marketing authorisation applications in the US, EU, and Japan.

Imaging schedule: baseline, then every 6 weeks until Week 48, then every 9 weeks until progression. All imaging is submitted for blinded independent central review (BICR).

sections.title: Background & Study Rationale
sections.contentHtml:
Despite the approval of pembrolizumab monotherapy for first-line metastatic NSCLC with PD-L1 TPS ≥50% (KEYNOTE-024), approximately half of participants progress within 10 months. Combination strategies that enhance anti-tumour immunity while targeting the tumour vasculature have shown promise.

Veloricept is a bispecific IgG1 antibody that simultaneously binds VEGFR2 (blocking angiogenic signalling) and PD-L1 (restoring effector T-cell function). The Phase 1b/2 VELORA-101 trial showed an ORR of 54% in previously untreated NSCLC with PD-L1 TPS ≥50% when veloricept was combined with pembrolizumab, versus a historical rate of ~45% for pembrolizumab monotherapy. The safety profile was manageable, with hypertension and proteinuria the principal class effects.

The present trial is designed to confirm these findings in a randomised Phase 3 setting against a contemporary active comparator.

sections.title: Objectives and Endpoints
sections.contentHtml:
Primary objective. To compare PFS between the experimental and comparator arms.

Primary endpoint. PFS by BICR per RECIST v1.1, defined as time from randomisation to the first documented radiographic progression or death from any cause, whichever occurs first.

Key secondary endpoints. (i) OS; (ii) ORR per RECIST v1.1 by BICR; (iii) DOR; (iv) safety per CTCAE v5.0; (v) PRO per EORTC QLQ-C30 and QLQ-LC13; (vi) PK and anti-drug antibodies.

sections.title: Study Design
sections.contentHtml:
Randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, active-controlled, parallel-group design. Participants are randomised 1:1 to Arm A (veloricept + pembrolizumab) or Arm B (pembrolizumab + platinum-doublet). Blinding is maintained via a double-dummy approach: all participants receive active IV veloricept or matching placebo, and investigator's-choice platinum-doublet chemotherapy or matching chemotherapy placebo (saline) for the first 4 cycles.

Treatment continues until confirmed radiographic progression, unacceptable toxicity, consent withdrawal, or completion of 35 cycles. The trial is event-driven; the primary PFS analysis occurs after 320 PFS events, and the final OS analysis after 410 OS events.

sections.title: Study Population (Inclusion/Exclusion)
sections.contentHtml:
Key inclusion criteria. Age ≥18 years; histologically or cytologically confirmed Stage IV NSCLC; no prior systemic therapy for metastatic disease; PD-L1 TPS ≥50% by central testing (Dako 22C3 pharmDx); ECOG PS 0–1; measurable disease per RECIST v1.1; adequate organ function; life expectancy ≥12 weeks.

Key exclusion criteria. Sensitising EGFR mutations or ALK/ROS1 rearrangements; untreated or symptomatic CNS metastases (treated, stable asymptomatic brain mets are permitted); active autoimmune disease requiring systemic therapy within 2 years; history of (non-infectious) pneumonitis requiring steroids; prior anti-PD-1/PD-L1/CTLA-4 therapy; uncontrolled hypertension (SBP >160 or DBP >100 mmHg); proteinuria ≥2+ or >1 g/24h at baseline; haemoptysis ≥2.5 mL within 4 weeks of randomisation; major surgery within 28 days.

sections.title: Method of Treatment Assignment & Blinding
sections.contentHtml:
Randomisation is performed centrally via an interactive web response system (IWRS) using a permuted-block scheme stratified by: (i) ECOG PS (0 vs 1); (ii) histology (squamous vs non-squamous); (iii) geographic region (US vs EU vs Japan). Allocation ratio is 1:1.

Participants, investigators, site staff, sponsor personnel involved in trial conduct, and the central imaging review vendor are blinded to treatment assignment. Unblinding is permitted only in medical emergencies via the IWRS 24/7 emergency unblinding function.

sections.title: Study Treatment
sections.contentHtml:
Veloricept. 15 mg/kg IV infusion over 60 minutes (first dose) or 30 minutes (subsequent doses) on Day 1 of each 3-week cycle. Supplied as 20 mg/mL solution in 500 mg single-dose vials.

Pembrolizumab. 200 mg IV infusion over 30 minutes on Day 1 of each 3-week cycle, after veloricept. Supplied per approved label (Keytruda, Merck Sharp & Dohme).

Platinum-doublet chemotherapy (Arm B only). Non-squamous: carboplatin AUC 5 + pemetrexed 500 mg/m² IV Day 1 every 3 weeks × 4 cycles, then pemetrexed maintenance. Squamous: carboplatin AUC 6 + paclitaxel 200 mg/m² IV Day 1 every 3 weeks × 4 cycles.

sections.title: Concomitant Therapy
sections.contentHtml:
Permitted concomitant therapies include supportive care medications (anti-emetics, analgesics, growth factors per ASCO/ESMO guidelines), bisphosphonates or denosumab for bone metastases, and palliative radiotherapy to non-target lesions.

Prohibited concomitant therapies include other systemic anti-cancer therapy; live-attenuated vaccines; chronic systemic corticosteroids >10 mg/day prednisone-equivalent (short courses for AE management are permitted); other investigational agents; and traditional/herbal medicines with known hepatotoxicity.

sections.title: Study Assessments
sections.contentHtml:
Scheduled assessments include: medical history, physical examination, vital signs, ECOG PS, CBC with differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, thyroid function tests, urinalysis with protein quantification, pregnancy testing (women of childbearing potential), 12-lead ECG, tumour imaging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis; MRI brain if indicated), and PRO questionnaires.

Pharmacokinetic sampling for veloricept occurs pre-dose and at end of infusion on C1D1, C2D1, C4D1, C8D1, and every 4 cycles thereafter. Anti-drug antibody samples are collected pre-dose on C1D1, C2D1, C4D1, C8D1, and at end-of-treatment.

sections.title: Assessment of Safety
sections.contentHtml:
Adverse events are coded to MedDRA v27.0 and graded per CTCAE v5.0. Serious adverse events (SAEs) are reported to the sponsor's pharmacovigilance department within 24 hours of site awareness. Suspected unexpected serious adverse reactions (SUSARs) are reported to regulators within the applicable local timelines per ICH E2A.

Adverse events of special interest (AESIs) include: immune-related AEs (pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis, endocrinopathies, nephritis, skin reactions, myocarditis); VEGF-pathway events (hypertension, proteinuria, haemorrhage, arterial/venous thromboembolism, GI perforation, wound-healing complications, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome); and infusion reactions.

sections.title: Statistical Considerations
sections.contentHtml:
With 320 PFS events, the trial has 90% power at a two-sided alpha of 0.05 to detect a hazard ratio of 0.70, assuming a median PFS of 10.3 months in the comparator arm. Alpha is split 0.025/0.025 between the interim and final analyses using O'Brien-Fleming boundaries.

OS testing is gated on PFS statistical significance; alpha is passed down hierarchically to OS, then ORR. The primary PFS analysis uses a stratified log-rank test; the hazard ratio is estimated from a stratified Cox model. Pre-specified sensitivity analyses include per-protocol analysis, investigator-assessed PFS, and censoring-rule variations.

sections.title: Data Collection, Management & QA
sections.contentHtml:
Electronic case report forms are built in Medidata Rave with range checks, cross-field edits, and auto-queries. Monitoring follows a risk-based model (RBM) per ICH E6(R3), with 100% source data verification (SDV) for the primary endpoint and 20% targeted SDV for secondary endpoints and safety data.

sections.title: Protocol Amendment Summary of Changes
sections.contentHtml:
Protocol Amendment 1 to VELORA-301 (Protocol v3.2) was finalised on 15 January 2024. The amendment introduces targeted changes to eligibility criteria, dosing guidance, and the statistical analysis plan without altering the primary study objective or primary endpoint.

Summary of changes: (i) expanded eligibility to permit treated, stable asymptomatic brain metastases (previously excluded); (ii) added dose modification guidance for Grade 2 proteinuria; (iii) added a pre-specified sensitivity analysis for PFS using a stratified test ignoring region (regulatory feedback from PMDA); (iv) added two interim safety reviews after 100 and 200 participants completed Cycle 4; (v) harmonised the assessment schedule between the European and Japanese sites.

sections.title: Rationale for Amendment
sections.contentHtml:
The amendment was triggered by three concurrent inputs: (1) a scientific advice letter from the EMA CHMP SAWP (dated 14 November 2023) recommending inclusion of patients with treated brain metastases, consistent with contemporary trial designs in NSCLC; (2) PMDA pre-submission consultation feedback (28 November 2023) requesting additional sensitivity analyses; (3) emerging VELORA-101 long-term safety data showing manageable low-grade proteinuria that benefits from early intervention.

No safety signal necessitated the amendment. All changes were classified as non-substantial under EU CTR 536/2014 Article 10 by the sponsor's regulatory team.

sections.title: Changes to Eligibility Criteria
sections.contentHtml:
Exclusion criterion 7 (previously: “any CNS metastases”) was revised to permit participants with brain metastases that have been definitively treated (surgical resection or stereotactic radiosurgery) at least 14 days before randomisation, are radiographically stable on imaging within 28 days of randomisation, and are not requiring corticosteroids >10 mg/day prednisone-equivalent for CNS symptoms.

No other eligibility criteria were modified. An approximate 8–12% increase in the eligible population was anticipated based on epidemiological estimates.

sections.title: Changes to Dosing Schedule
sections.contentHtml: No change to the primary dosing of veloricept (15 mg/kg every 3 weeks) or pembrolizumab (200 mg every 3 weeks). The dose modification table in Appendix 3 was expanded to include guidance for Grade 2 proteinuria: hold veloricept until protein <2 g/24h, then resume at the same dose; permanent discontinuation only for recurrent Grade 3 proteinuria or any episode of nephrotic syndrome.

sections.title: Updated Statistical Analysis Plan
sections.contentHtml: Section 14 (Statistical Considerations) was updated to add two pre-specified sensitivity analyses: (i) stratified log-rank test ignoring region (addressing a PMDA request on regional heterogeneity); (ii) a tipping-point analysis evaluating the robustness of the PFS primary analysis to assumed missing-at-random assumptions. The primary analysis population, test, and alpha allocation were unchanged.

sections.title: Updated Assessment Schedule
sections.contentHtml: The assessment schedule in Section 12 was clarified to align the Week 6 and Week 12 imaging timepoints across all regions (previously ambiguous for Japanese sites, where some imaging had drifted to the +/- 3-day window). Two additional interim safety reviews were added at approximately 100 and 200 participants post-Cycle 4 to supplement the existing IDMC schedule.

sections.title: Patient Narrative (chronological prose)
sections.contentHtml:
Participant 047-0042 is a 68-year-old male former smoker (45 pack-years, quit 2015) with Stage IV adenocarcinoma of the right upper lobe, PD-L1 TPS 85%, ECOG PS 1, randomised to Arm A on 18 April 2024 and treated with veloricept 15 mg/kg + pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks. He completed Cycles 1–6 without significant toxicity, with best response of partial response confirmed at the Week 12 scan.

On 15 August 2024 (Day 120, 11 days after Cycle 6), the participant developed progressive dry cough, exertional dyspnoea, and low-grade fever (37.9 °C). He presented to the clinic on 17 August 2024. SpO₂ was 90% on room air (baseline 97%). High-resolution CT demonstrated bilateral patchy ground-glass opacities with upper-lobe predominance, consistent with drug-induced pneumonitis. Bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for infection (bacterial, fungal, PCP, viral). SARS-CoV-2 and influenza PCR were negative. Pulmonary consult diagnosed probable Grade 3 immune-related pneumonitis.

Study treatment was permanently discontinued on 17 August 2024. The participant was admitted and started on intravenous methylprednisolone 2 mg/kg/day. Oxygen was weaned over 5 days. He was discharged on 22 August 2024 on an oral prednisone taper (1 mg/kg) over 8 weeks. At the follow-up visit on 05 October 2024, symptoms were resolving, SpO₂ was 95% on room air, and repeat HRCT showed partial resolution of the ground-glass opacities.

sections.title: Causality Considerations
sections.contentHtml:
Alternative aetiologies were systematically excluded: infection (negative BAL cultures, negative viral PCR panel including SARS-CoV-2 and influenza, negative galactomannan and PCP PCR); disease progression (concurrent CT showed stable target lesions, no new lesions); radiation pneumonitis (no history of thoracic radiotherapy); cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (normal BNP, normal echocardiogram); concomitant-medication-related ILD (no concomitant drugs with established ILD association).

The clinical picture (subacute bilateral ground-glass opacities, upper-lobe predominance, response to high-dose corticosteroids) is highly characteristic of immune checkpoint inhibitor pneumonitis. The temporal relationship (onset 11 days after C6, cumulative pembrolizumab exposure 1,200 mg) and the known Reference Safety Information for pembrolizumab (pneumonitis incidence ~4–5% in monotherapy, higher in combinations) support probable causality for pembrolizumab. The role of veloricept is less well characterised; a contribution cannot be excluded, hence possible causality is assigned. The event is expected per the current Investigator's Brochure and does not qualify as a SUSAR.

sections.title: Executive Summary
sections.contentHtml:
This is the second Development Safety Update Report (DSUR) for veloricept, covering the Development International Birth Date (DIBD) anniversary period 01 October 2023 to 30 September 2024. Across the global clinical development programme, 1,247 participants had received at least one dose of veloricept by data cutoff. The pivotal VELORA-301 Phase 3 trial completed enrolment during this period (612 randomised, 303 treated with veloricept) and the pre-planned PFS interim analysis was positive.

No new safety signals were identified. Known risks (hypertension, proteinuria, immune-related pneumonitis, haemorrhage, infusion reactions) remain within expected rates. The sponsor concludes that the benefit-risk profile of veloricept remains favourable, and no changes to the Reference Safety Information are proposed in this reporting period.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.contentHtml:
Veloricept (GBC-204) is a humanised bispecific IgG1 monoclonal antibody targeting VEGFR2 and PD-L1, under development by GenBioCa Oncology, Inc. for the treatment of multiple solid tumours. The Development International Birth Date (DIBD) is 01 October 2022, corresponding to the first dose administered in the first-in-human VELORA-101 trial.

This Year 2 DSUR covers the period 01 October 2023 to 30 September 2024 and is prepared in accordance with ICH E2F.

Scientific advice was obtained from the EMA CHMP SAWP (letter dated 14 November 2023) and PMDA (pre-submission consultation, 28 November 2023) during the reporting period.

sections.title: Significant Findings from Clinical Trials
sections.contentHtml:
The most clinically significant finding during the reporting period was the positive pre-planned PFS interim analysis of VELORA-301 (data cutoff 30 September 2024). Full efficacy and safety results are reported in DOC-001. In brief, the safety profile observed in the Phase 3 setting was consistent with the known profiles of veloricept monotherapy and pembrolizumab monotherapy; no new signals emerged in the combination setting.

Notably, the rate of Grade ≥3 immune-related pneumonitis in the veloricept + pembrolizumab arm (3.0%) is slightly higher than historical pembrolizumab monotherapy rates (approximately 2.0% per label), consistent with the expected additive effect of a PD-L1 arm of the bispecific. This remains within the Reference Safety Information.

sections.title: Safety Findings from Non-interventional Studies
sections.contentHtml: No non-interventional safety studies of veloricept were ongoing during the reporting period. Post-marketing commitments and PASS/PAES planning will commence after first regulatory approval.

sections.title: Non-clinical Data
sections.contentHtml: No new non-clinical safety findings were identified during the reporting period. A chronic (26-week) toxicology study in cynomolgus monkey completed in-life during Q2 2024; final report expected Q1 2025. Preliminary findings showed reversible, non-adverse changes in the kidney (minimal glomerular changes consistent with VEGF-pathway inhibition) at the highest dose; no new target organs identified.

sections.title: Literature
sections.contentHtml: A literature search (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library) covering 01 October 2023 to 30 September 2024 using the search strategy “veloricept OR GBC-204 OR ‘VEGFR2 PD-L1 bispecific’” identified 7 relevant publications: 3 preclinical, 2 Phase 1b/2 reports from VELORA-101, 1 narrative review of VEGF/immune combinations in NSCLC, and 1 editorial. No new safety information not already addressed in sponsor-held data was identified.

sections.title: Other DSURs
sections.contentHtml: No other DSURs for veloricept were submitted during this reporting period. This Year 2 DSUR is the sole active periodic safety report for the molecule.

sections.title: Lack of Efficacy
sections.contentHtml: No evidence of lack of efficacy raising safety concerns was identified during the reporting period. The pre-planned VELORA-301 PFS interim analysis crossed the efficacy boundary (HR 0.62, p<0.0001). The ongoing VELORA-202 trial in hepatocellular carcinoma remains blinded; no futility signal has been identified by the IDMC.

sections.title: Region-Specific Information
sections.contentHtml: Region-specific safety communications during the reporting period were limited to: (i) a sponsor-initiated Dear Investigator Letter (06 March 2024) to Japanese sites clarifying the proteinuria management algorithm; (ii) a sponsor response to a PMDA post-consultation inquiry regarding Asian-subgroup PK (dated 12 July 2024). No regional regulatory safety actions occurred.

sections.title: Late-Breaking Information
sections.contentHtml: No late-breaking information between the data cutoff (30 September 2024) and the DSUR submission date (planned 15 December 2024) has emerged that would alter the conclusions of this report.

sections.title: Overall Safety Assessment
sections.contentHtml: Overall, the safety profile of veloricept remains consistent with the risks characterised in the Reference Safety Information. Key risks (hypertension, proteinuria, immune-related pneumonitis, haemorrhage, infusion reactions) occurred at rates within or below expected ranges. The addition of veloricept to pembrolizumab in the VELORA-301 trial increased the rate of VEGF-pathway toxicities (hypertension, proteinuria) as anticipated by mechanism, but these were manageable with established interventions, and the overall tolerability was favourable relative to the pembrolizumab + platinum-doublet comparator.

sections.title: Summary of Important Risks
sections.contentHtml: Important identified risks: hypertension; proteinuria; infusion reactions; immune-related adverse events (pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis, endocrinopathies, nephritis). Important potential risks: haemorrhage (including pulmonary haemorrhage); arterial and venous thromboembolism; gastrointestinal perforation; wound-healing complications; posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES); embryo-foetal toxicity; immunogenicity. Missing information: safety in paediatric populations; safety in participants with Child-Pugh B/C hepatic impairment; safety in long-term (>2 years) exposure.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.contentHtml: The benefit-risk balance of veloricept remains favourable. No new safety signals warranting a change to the Reference Safety Information, protocol modifications, or regulatory action were identified during the reporting period. The sponsor will continue cumulative safety monitoring and submit the next DSUR by 31 December 2025.

sections.title: Summary
sections.contentHtml:
Veloricept is a humanised IgG4 monoclonal antibody targeting Delta-like ligand 4 (DLL4) on tumour-associated endothelium, interrupting Notch-mediated angiogenesis. The clinical programme is positioned in advanced non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) in combination with the PD-1 inhibitor pembrolizumab, where preclinical and Phase 1b data demonstrate complementary vascular normalisation and T-cell priming.

As of 2024-09-30, 612 participants have been exposed to veloricept across six studies (Ph1 dose-escalation, Ph1b combination, Ph2 ICI-combo, and the ongoing Ph3 VELORA-301). The most frequent (≥10%) adverse events are hypertension, fatigue, headache, and transaminase elevation, generally Grade 1–2. Serious angiogenesis-class signals (bleeding, GI perforation, delayed wound healing) remain within rates reported for other anti-angiogenic agents.

Veloricept 10 mg/kg IV every 3 weeks is the recommended Phase 3 dose, selected based on exposure-response analyses from Study VLR-102 and PK/PD modelling.

sections.title: Introduction and Development Rationale
sections.contentHtml:
Despite the addition of PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) to platinum doublets, approximately 60% of patients with metastatic NSCLC either fail to respond or develop acquired resistance within 12 months. Tumour vasculature contributes to immune escape via hypoxia-driven immunosuppression, impaired T-cell infiltration, and VEGF-mediated recruitment of regulatory T cells.

DLL4 blockade preferentially targets the tumour endothelium rather than normal vasculature, reducing the risk of hypertension and proteinuria seen with VEGF-pathway inhibitors while promoting vessel normalisation that enhances CD8+ T-cell infiltration (Benedito 2009; Kuhnert 2011). The scientific rationale for combination with pembrolizumab is to convert “cold” immune-excluded tumours into inflamed, ICI-responsive microenvironments.

sections.title: Physical, Chemical, and Pharmaceutical Properties
sections.contentHtml:
Veloricept is a recombinant humanised IgG4κ monoclonal antibody produced in Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells. Molecular weight 148.6 kDa. The drug product is supplied as a sterile, preservative-free, clear-to-slightly-opalescent liquid in single-use 20 mL glass vials at a concentration of 25 mg/mL.

  • Excipients: histidine buffer (pH 6.0), trehalose dihydrate, polysorbate 80.
  • Storage: 2–8 °C protected from light; do not freeze or shake.
  • In-use stability: 24 h at 2–8 °C or 8 h at room temperature after dilution in 0.9% saline.

sections.title: Non-clinical Studies
sections.contentHtml:
Pharmacology (in vitro): veloricept binds human DLL4 with KD = 0.21 nM and blocks DLL4–Notch1 interaction (IC50 = 0.9 nM). No measurable cross-reactivity with DLL1 or JAG1/2.

Pharmacology (in vivo): dose-dependent tumour-growth inhibition in H1975 (EGFR L858R/T790M) and LLC1 syngeneic NSCLC models at 5–20 mg/kg IP twice weekly. Combination with anti-PD-1 (RMP1-14) produced synergistic T-cell infiltration (CD8/Treg ratio increased 3.2-fold vs anti-PD-1 alone).

Toxicology: 13-week GLP studies in cynomolgus monkeys (highest non-severely-toxic dose 50 mg/kg weekly) identified reversible dose-dependent reductions in reticulocyte count and transient transaminase elevations. No cardiac, renal, or reproductive findings.

sections.title: Clinical Pharmacology
sections.contentHtml:
Veloricept exhibits linear pharmacokinetics over the 1–20 mg/kg dose range with a terminal half-life of 18–21 days consistent with FcRn-mediated recycling. Steady-state is achieved by cycle 4 of Q3W dosing.

Population PK modelling (NONMEM, n = 248) identified body weight, baseline albumin, and tumour burden (sum of RECIST target lesions) as covariates on clearance. Exposure (AUCss) is predicted to be ≥80% of target in >95% of patients at 10 mg/kg Q3W, supporting a flat dose for Phase 3 operational simplicity.

No clinically meaningful PK interactions observed when co-administered with pembrolizumab, platinum doublets, or docetaxel.

sections.title: Clinical Efficacy
sections.contentHtml:
Phase 1b (VLR-102) in heavily pretreated NSCLC (n = 48): confirmed ORR 23% (95% CI 12–38) with veloricept monotherapy, 41% (95% CI 25–59) in combination with pembrolizumab. Median duration of response not reached at 14 months of follow-up.

Phase 2 (VLR-201) in first-line ICI-eligible NSCLC (n = 124, randomised 1:1 veloricept+pembrolizumab vs pembrolizumab alone): median PFS 11.4 vs 7.1 months (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.42–0.91, p = 0.014); 24-month OS 51% vs 36%. These data support the hypothesis tested in the pivotal VELORA-301 trial.

sections.title: Clinical Safety
sections.contentHtml:
Safety database (n = 612 veloricept-exposed as of 2024-09-30). The most common treatment-emergent adverse events (any grade, ≥10%) are:

  • Hypertension — 24% (Grade 3 7%)
  • Fatigue — 31% (Grade 3 2%)
  • Headache — 18% (Grade 3 <1%)
  • ALT/AST elevation — 15% (Grade 3 3%)
  • Proteinuria — 11% (Grade 3 <1%)

Immune-related AEs when combined with pembrolizumab mirror the pembrolizumab monotherapy label; pneumonitis incidence (any grade) is 6% vs 4% expected for pembrolizumab alone — investigators are reminded to maintain high index of suspicion.

Fatal AEs attributable to veloricept: 4 of 612 (0.65%); causes GI perforation (2), pulmonary haemorrhage (1), hepatic failure (1).

sections.title: Reference Safety Information
sections.contentHtml:
The following events are considered expected for veloricept and will be used by the sponsor's PV function to determine expectedness of SUSARs per ICH E2A:

  • Hypertension (all grades)
  • Proteinuria (all grades)
  • Transaminase elevation (Grade 1–3)
  • Delayed wound healing
  • Mucosal bleeding (epistaxis, gingival)
  • Fatigue
  • Infusion-related reactions
  • Reversible asymptomatic reduction in reticulocyte count

Events not on this list, if assessed as related to veloricept and resulting in SAE criteria, must be reported as SUSAR within applicable timelines (7-day/15-day).

sections.title: Guidance for the Investigator
sections.contentHtml:
Infusion administration: dilute veloricept in 100 mL 0.9% sodium chloride; infuse IV over 60 min via a 0.2–0.22 µm low-protein-binding in-line filter. Do not administer as IV push.

Blood pressure monitoring: measure BP prior to each infusion. For sustained BP ≥140/90 mmHg, initiate anti-hypertensive therapy per site standard of care; dose interruption is not required unless Grade 3 persists >7 days despite therapy.

Hepatic monitoring: ALT/AST and bilirubin every cycle. Hold veloricept for ALT or AST >5× ULN; permanently discontinue for >20× ULN or Hy's Law criteria.

Immune-related pneumonitis (combination arm): any new or worsening dyspnoea, cough, or chest imaging infiltrate must trigger diagnostic workup including HRCT. Grade 2 or higher pneumonitis: hold both veloricept and pembrolizumab, initiate corticosteroids per the pembrolizumab USPI.

sections.title: Overview and Key Information
sections.contentHtml:
You are being asked to take part in a research study. This form explains what the study is about so you can decide if you want to join. Please read it carefully. You can ask the study doctor any questions you have before you decide.

Key points you should know:

  • This study is for people with a kind of lung cancer called non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that has spread to other parts of the body.
  • You will get one of two treatment combinations, assigned by chance (like flipping a coin). You will not know which one you are getting.
  • Taking part is your choice. If you say no, your regular care will not change.
  • You can stop at any time, for any reason, without losing any of your rights.

sections.title: Why is this study being done?
sections.contentHtml:
This study is being done to see if adding a new medicine called veloricept to a medicine called pembrolizumab works better than giving pembrolizumab plus the usual chemotherapy for your type of lung cancer.

Pembrolizumab is already approved to treat your type of cancer. Veloricept is new and has not been approved by the FDA or other agencies. The sponsor — GenBioCa Oncology — believes veloricept may help pembrolizumab work better, but we need to study it in people like you to know for sure.

sections.title: What is the usual approach to my condition?
sections.contentHtml: The usual treatment for your condition is pembrolizumab, sometimes combined with chemotherapy. These medicines help your immune system attack the cancer and can slow the cancer or shrink it. On average, the cancer stays controlled for about 10 months with pembrolizumab alone, but this varies a lot from person to person.

sections.title: What are my choices if I decide not to take part?
sections.contentHtml:
If you decide not to join this study, you can still receive the usual treatment for your cancer. Your study doctor can talk with you about other treatment choices, which may include:

  • Pembrolizumab by itself
  • Pembrolizumab combined with chemotherapy
  • Chemotherapy by itself
  • Supportive care (treatment to help you feel better even if we are not treating the cancer directly)
  • Another clinical trial, if available at your centre

sections.title: What will happen if I decide to take part?
sections.contentHtml:
If you decide to join:

  • We will first do screening tests (physical exam, blood tests, scans, heart tracing) over about 4 weeks to make sure the study is right for you.
  • If you qualify, you will be assigned by chance to one of two treatment groups.
  • You will come to the clinic every 3 weeks to get your treatment through a vein (IV). This takes about 2–3 hours each visit.
  • Every 6 weeks (and later every 9 weeks) you will have a CT scan to see how the cancer is responding.
  • You will continue treatment for up to 2 years, as long as it is helping and you can tolerate it.
  • After you stop, we will check in with you every 3 months to see how you are doing.

sections.title: What are the risks and benefits?
sections.contentHtml:
Possible benefits. We cannot promise that this study will help you. It is possible that the new combination may slow your cancer more than the usual treatment, but it may also work the same or less well. Information from this study may help future people with the same cancer.

Possible risks. Common side effects (more than 1 in 10 people) include: feeling tired, cough, feeling sick to your stomach, decreased appetite, high blood pressure, protein in your urine, and skin rash. Serious but less common risks (less than 1 in 20 people) include: inflammation of the lungs (pneumonitis), inflammation of the liver (hepatitis), inflammation of the gut (colitis), problems with thyroid or adrenal glands, bleeding, blood clots, infusion reactions, and — rarely — death.

You will be monitored closely at every visit for side effects. Most side effects can be managed with medicines or by pausing treatment.

sections.title: Can I stop later?
sections.contentHtml:
Yes. Taking part is completely voluntary. You can stop the study at any time, for any reason, without any penalty and without losing any benefits you would otherwise receive. If you stop, we would like to continue following you with phone calls or clinic visits so we can learn how you are doing — but even that is your choice.

Your study doctor may also stop your treatment if they believe it is in your best interest (for example, if the cancer gets worse or if side effects become too severe).

sections.title: What are the study groups?
sections.contentHtml:
There are two study groups. You will be assigned by chance (1 in 2 chance of each) to one of them. Neither you nor your doctor will know which group you are in until the study is unblinded (usually when it is complete).

  • Group A: Veloricept (the new medicine) + pembrolizumab, every 3 weeks by IV.
  • Group B: Pembrolizumab + chemotherapy (either carboplatin + pemetrexed, or carboplatin + paclitaxel, depending on your cancer type), every 3 weeks by IV for 4 cycles, then pembrolizumab by itself (sometimes with pemetrexed).

sections.title: Exams, tests, and procedures involved
sections.contentHtml:
During the study, you will have:

  • Physical exams and health history at each visit
  • Blood tests (full blood count, kidney and liver tests, thyroid tests) every 3 weeks
  • Urine tests every 3 weeks
  • CT scans of your chest, belly, and pelvis every 6 weeks for the first year, then every 9 weeks
  • MRI of your brain if your doctor thinks it is needed
  • Heart tracing (ECG) at screening and sometimes later
  • Pregnancy test (if you can become pregnant) at screening and periodically
  • Questionnaires about how you are feeling (about 15 minutes, every 6 weeks)

sections.title: What are my responsibilities?
sections.contentHtml:
If you join, you agree to:

  • Come to all scheduled visits as closely as possible
  • Tell the study team about any new symptoms or health changes
  • Tell the study team about any new medicines or supplements you start, including herbal remedies
  • Use effective birth control during the study and for 4 months after your last dose, if you are of childbearing potential (or if your partner is)
  • Not take part in any other clinical trial while you are in this one

sections.title: What are the costs?
sections.contentHtml:
You will not have to pay for the study drugs (veloricept and pembrolizumab) or for study-specific tests and scans. Your insurance (or Medicare/Medicaid) may be billed for standard care that you would have had anyway, such as routine visits and basic blood tests. The study will reimburse reasonable travel costs (parking, mileage, meals) up to $75 per visit; your site coordinator can give you details.

You will not be paid for taking part in the study.

sections.title: What if I am injured?
sections.contentHtml:
If you are injured as a direct result of taking part in this study, the sponsor (GenBioCa Oncology, Inc.) will pay for medical care that is reasonable and necessary to treat the injury, to the extent not covered by your health insurance. You do not give up any of your legal rights by signing this form.

Call the study doctor right away if you think you may have been injured because of the study: Dr. Elena Vázquez, (212) 555-0147 (24/7).

sections.title: Who will see my medical information?
sections.contentHtml:
Information collected about you during the study will be shared with: the study doctor and site staff; the sponsor (GenBioCa) and its contractors; the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and other health authorities; and your institution's IRB. We will protect your privacy by using a study code number instead of your name on all study records sent outside your site.

Your de-identified data (data with your name and direct identifiers removed) may be used for future research. Results of the study may be published in medical journals or presented at conferences, but you will not be identified. Your records are protected under US HIPAA (and the applicable local privacy law for non-US sites).

sections.contentHtml:
If you have questions about the study at any time, call the study doctor: Dr. Elena Vázquez, Site 047 (Memorial Sloan Kettering), (212) 555-0147.

If you have questions about your rights as a research participant, or if you want to report a concern about how the study is being conducted, call the MSK Institutional Review Board at (212) 555-7777 or email irb@mskcc.org.

For general information about clinical trials, visit www.ClinicalTrials.gov and search for NCT05472194.

sections.title: Title Page
sections.contentHtml:
Clinical Study Report. Protocol SPINE-TB-2. A Phase 3, Open-Label, Randomised, Multicentre, Non-Inferiority Trial of a 9-Month Levofloxacin-Based Regimen versus the Standard 12-Month Regimen (2HRZE/10HRE) for Rifampicin-Sensitive Spinal Tuberculosis (Pott's Disease) in Adults and Adolescents.

Report Version 0.2. Data cutoff: 30 June 2026. Sponsor: GenBioCa India Pvt. Ltd. Coordinating centre: All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi. Date of this report: 14 August 2026. Report prepared in accordance with ICH E3.

sections.title: Synopsis
sections.contentHtml:
Objective. To determine whether a 9-month levofloxacin-based regimen is non-inferior to the WHO-standard 12-month regimen for the treatment of rifampicin-sensitive spinal tuberculosis.

Methods. Open-label, randomised (1:1), multicentre, non-inferiority Phase 3 trial. 684 participants were randomised across 24 sites in India (16), South Africa (3), the Philippines (3), and Brazil (2).

Primary results. At 12 months post-therapy, treatment success (per CDSCO-aligned composite endpoint) was achieved in 86.4% (293/339) of the 9-month arm versus 88.1% (304/345) of the 12-month arm; adjusted difference −1.7 percentage points (95% CI −6.4 to +3.0). The upper bound of the 95% CI was within the pre-specified non-inferiority margin of 8 percentage points, meeting the primary objective.

Conclusions. The 9-month levofloxacin-based regimen was non-inferior to the standard 12-month regimen with respect to treatment success, with a comparable safety profile and improved treatment completion rates.

sections.title: Ethics
sections.contentHtml:
The trial was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki (2013), ICH E6(R3) GCP, and applicable national regulations: India — New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules 2019 and the ICMR National Ethical Guidelines (2017); South Africa — SAHPRA Clinical Trial Regulations; Philippines — FDA Philippines; Brazil — ANVISA RDC 9/2015 and CONEP.

Independent ethics committee approval was obtained at every site before enrolment. Written informed consent was obtained in the participant's preferred language from a validated translation; thumbprint consent with impartial witness was used for illiterate participants per NDCT Rules 2019.

sections.title: Investigators & Sites
sections.contentHtml:
The trial was conducted at 24 sites: 16 in India (AIIMS Delhi; AIIMS Rishikesh; CMC Vellore; KEM Mumbai; PGIMER Chandigarh; NIRT Chennai; and 10 secondary-care tertiary centres); 3 in South Africa (University of Cape Town, Stellenbosch, Wits); 3 in the Philippines (Lung Center of the Philippines, PGH Manila, Davao Medical Center); 2 in Brazil (Instituto Nacional de Infectologia Evandro Chagas, FIOCRUZ; Hospital das Clínicas São Paulo).

The coordinating principal investigator was Prof. Priya Ramasubramaniam (AIIMS New Delhi). The Independent Data and Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) comprised a thoracic physician (chair), a hepatologist, a biostatistician, and a lay patient representative.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.contentHtml:
Spinal tuberculosis (Pott's disease) accounts for approximately 1–3% of all TB cases globally and 50% of musculoskeletal TB. India bears the highest absolute burden (~70,000 incident cases per year). The historical reference for duration of therapy is the Medical Research Council Working Party on Tuberculosis of the Spine (MRC 1998, Pattison), which supported 9-month regimens but was conducted before standardised rifampicin-based short-course chemotherapy was widely adopted.

WHO currently recommends 12 months of therapy (2HRZE/10HRE) for spinal TB, extrapolated from pulmonary TB guidelines. There is renewed clinical interest in shorter regimens, particularly given the strong tissue penetration of fluoroquinolones. SPINE-TB-2 was designed to test whether a 9-month regimen incorporating levofloxacin can preserve efficacy while improving adherence and reducing cumulative toxicity.

sections.title: Study Objectives
sections.contentHtml:
Primary objective. To demonstrate non-inferiority (margin 8 percentage points) of a 9-month levofloxacin-based regimen versus the WHO-standard 12-month regimen for treatment success at 12 months post-therapy in participants with rifampicin-sensitive spinal TB.

Key secondary objectives. (i) Culture conversion at Month 2 and Month 4; (ii) time to pain-free weight bearing; (iii) radiological healing per Bhojraj grading at Month 9 and Month 18; (iv) treatment completion rate; (v) relapse at 24 months; (vi) safety and tolerability, with special focus on hepatotoxicity and QT prolongation.

sections.title: Investigational Plan
sections.contentHtml:
Participants were randomised 1:1 to Arm A (experimental, 9-month regimen: 2 months of levofloxacin + isoniazid + rifampicin + pyrazinamide, followed by 7 months of levofloxacin + isoniazid + rifampicin, all as weight-banded fixed-dose combination tablets) or Arm B (control, standard 12-month regimen per WHO: 2HRZE/10HRE).

Randomisation was stratified by site, severity (Pott's paraplegia present vs absent), and HIV status (positive vs negative). All participants received NTEP-aligned supportive care (pyridoxine, surgical referral for neurological compromise, nutritional supplementation). Follow-up continued for 24 months after treatment start.

sections.title: Efficacy Evaluation (culture conversion + radiological healing)
sections.contentHtml:
Primary efficacy analysis was performed on the modified ITT (mITT) population (all randomised participants who received at least one dose of ATT; 684 total). The primary endpoint was a composite “treatment success” at 12 months post-therapy, defined per CDSCO as: (a) absence of culture-positive relapse; (b) absence of radiological progression; (c) no need for salvage therapy for TB; and (d) no TB-related death.

At 12 months post-therapy, treatment success was observed in 86.4% (293/339) of Arm A versus 88.1% (304/345) of Arm B; adjusted difference −1.7 percentage points (95% CI −6.4 to +3.0). The upper bound of the 95% CI was within the pre-specified non-inferiority margin of 8 percentage points, demonstrating non-inferiority (p<0.001 for non-inferiority).

Secondary endpoints: Month 2 culture conversion was 78.2% (Arm A) vs 76.4% (Arm B); time to pain-free weight bearing (median) was 4.6 vs 5.2 months (p=0.03 favouring Arm A); radiological healing (Bhojraj grade III/IV) at Month 18 was 82.6% vs 83.9% (p=0.65). Treatment completion was 92.6% in Arm A vs 85.5% in Arm B (p=0.004).

sections.title: Safety Evaluation (hepatotoxicity focus)
sections.contentHtml:
Safety was assessed in all participants who received at least one dose (safety population: 339 Arm A, 345 Arm B). AEs were coded to MedDRA v27.0 and graded per CTCAE v5.0.

Any TEAE occurred in 84.1% (Arm A) vs 86.4% (Arm B). Grade ≥3 TEAEs occurred in 18.6% vs 22.9%, respectively. The most common Grade ≥3 AEs were drug-induced hepatitis (Arm A 8.3%, Arm B 11.3%), peripheral neuropathy (Arm A 2.4%, Arm B 3.5%), and QT prolongation (Arm A 1.2%, Arm B 0.3%).

sections.title: Discussion & Conclusions
sections.contentHtml:
SPINE-TB-2 met its primary objective, demonstrating non-inferiority of a 9-month levofloxacin-based regimen versus the WHO-standard 12-month regimen for treatment success at 12 months post-therapy. The adjusted risk difference (−1.7 pp; 95% CI −6.4 to +3.0) was well within the pre-specified 8 percentage-point margin. The result was consistent across the mITT and per-protocol populations and across all pre-specified subgroups (HIV status, Pott's paraplegia, country, diabetes).

Treatment completion was significantly higher in the 9-month arm (92.6% vs 85.5%; p=0.004), supporting the operational benefit of the shorter regimen. Safety was comparable between arms; hepatotoxicity rates (the dominant class-wide risk) were numerically lower in Arm A. The expected fluoroquinolone-class signals (QT prolongation, tendinopathy) occurred at low frequencies and were manageable.

These findings support revision of national (NTEP) and international (WHO) treatment guidelines for rifampicin-sensitive spinal TB to permit a 9-month levofloxacin-based regimen, with monthly LFT and ECG monitoring, as a programmatic alternative to the current 12-month regimen.

sections.contentHtml:

Protocol Identifier: SPINE-TB-2. CTRI Registration: CTRI/2023/06/054218. Sponsor: GenBioCa India Pvt. Ltd. Coordinating centre: AIIMS, New Delhi.

sections.title: Study Centre(s)
sections.contentHtml: Twenty-four (24) investigational sites across 4 countries: India (16 sites — including AIIMS New Delhi, AIIMS Rishikesh, CMC Vellore, KEM Mumbai, PGIMER Chandigarh, NIRT Chennai, and 10 regional tertiary centres); South Africa (3 sites); Philippines (3 sites); Brazil (2 sites).

sections.contentHtml: Primary publication is planned in The Lancet Infectious Diseases with simultaneous presentation at the World Conference on Lung Health (The Union, 2026). Reference literature includes the MRC 1998 Working Party on Tuberculosis of the Spine (Int Orthop 1999;23:73–81) and the WHO Consolidated Guidelines on Tuberculosis (2022).

sections.title: Study Period (Dates)
sections.contentHtml: First participant randomised: 15 July 2023. Last participant randomised: 28 February 2025. Primary endpoint analysis cutoff (last participant 12-month post-therapy visit): 30 June 2026. Database lock: 20 July 2026. 24-month safety and relapse follow-up continues through Q1 2028.

sections.title: Phase of Development
sections.contentHtml: Phase 3, pivotal registration trial supporting submissions to CDSCO (India), SAHPRA (South Africa), FDA Philippines, and ANVISA (Brazil). The trial is designed to inform revision of the NTEP (India) and WHO guidelines on spinal TB treatment duration.

sections.title: Objectives
sections.contentHtml:
Primary. Non-inferiority of a 9-month levofloxacin-based regimen vs the WHO-standard 12-month regimen for treatment success at 12 months post-therapy (margin: 8 percentage points).

Key secondary. Early culture conversion (Month 2, Month 4); time to pain-free weight bearing; radiological healing (Bhojraj grading) at Month 9 and Month 18; treatment completion rates; relapse at 24 months; safety (hepatotoxicity, QT, peripheral neuropathy, tendinopathy).

sections.title: Methodology / Study Design
sections.contentHtml: Open-label, randomised (1:1), active-controlled, parallel-group, multicentre, non-inferiority Phase 3 trial. Randomisation was stratified by site, Pott's paraplegia (present vs absent), and HIV status. Participants and investigators were not blinded given the differences in regimen duration and pill burden; however, outcome assessors (microbiologists, radiologists reading Bhojraj grading, independent adjudicators) were blinded to treatment allocation.

sections.title: Number of Subjects (Planned & Analysed)
sections.contentHtml: Planned: 672 participants (336 per arm). Analysed: 684 randomised (339 Arm A, 345 Arm B); 684 included in the mITT (safety and primary efficacy) population. Enrolment slightly exceeded target to compensate for anticipated loss-to-follow-up in operationally challenging sites.

sections.title: Diagnosis & Main Criteria for Inclusion
sections.contentHtml: Adults and adolescents (age ≥14 years) with newly diagnosed, previously untreated spinal (vertebral) tuberculosis, with microbiological confirmation (Xpert MTB/RIF or culture) OR a composite clinical/radiological/histopathological diagnosis consistent with CDSCO case-definition guidance. Rifampicin sensitivity by Xpert MTB/RIF (or phenotypic DST where Xpert not performed) was required.

sections.title: Test Product, Dose & Mode of Administration
sections.contentHtml: Arm A (experimental). 2 months of levofloxacin (750 mg daily) + isoniazid + rifampicin + pyrazinamide (per weight band, fixed-dose combination tablets), followed by 7 months of levofloxacin + isoniazid + rifampicin. Total duration: 9 months. All medicines administered orally once daily under NTEP-aligned adherence support (DOTS/DAT where available).

sections.title: Duration of Treatment
sections.contentHtml: Arm A: 9 months. Arm B: 12 months. Treatment duration was fixed by protocol regardless of radiological or microbiological response, mirroring programmatic conditions.

sections.title: Reference Therapy
sections.contentHtml: WHO-standard regimen for drug-sensitive TB: 2 months of isoniazid + rifampicin + pyrazinamide + ethambutol (2HRZE) followed by 10 months of isoniazid + rifampicin + ethambutol (10HRE), per the WHO Consolidated Guidelines on Tuberculosis (2022) and the Indian NTEP Technical and Operational Guidelines (2023).

sections.title: Criteria for Evaluation (Efficacy / Safety)
sections.contentHtml:
Efficacy. Composite treatment success at 12 months post-therapy per CDSCO definition (absence of relapse, radiological progression, salvage therapy, or TB death). Culture conversion assessed monthly for the first 4 months. Radiological healing assessed via Bhojraj grading (I–IV) on MRI at Baseline, Month 9, and Month 18.

Safety. AEs coded to MedDRA v27.0, graded per CTCAE v5.0. Monthly LFTs (hepatotoxicity surveillance), monthly ECG for QT monitoring, baseline + 6-monthly ophthalmology (optic neuritis screening).

sections.title: Statistical Methods
sections.contentHtml: Primary analysis: Miettinen-Nurminen-based 95% CI around the adjusted risk difference, with non-inferiority declared if the upper 95% CI bound was below the +8 percentage-point margin. Analyses were performed on the mITT and per-protocol populations with concordance between the two required for a positive conclusion. The target sample size (672) provided 85% power at a one-sided alpha of 0.025 to declare non-inferiority assuming a true difference of 0 and a control-arm success rate of 85%.

sections.title: Summary of Efficacy Results
sections.contentHtml: Treatment success at 12 months post-therapy: 86.4% Arm A vs 88.1% Arm B; adjusted difference −1.7 pp (95% CI −6.4 to +3.0; p<0.001 for non-inferiority). Per-protocol analysis consistent (adjusted difference −2.0 pp; 95% CI −6.8 to +2.8). Month 2 culture conversion 78.2% vs 76.4%. Time to pain-free weight bearing median 4.6 vs 5.2 months (p=0.03). Bhojraj grade III/IV at Month 18: 82.6% vs 83.9% (p=0.65). Treatment completion 92.6% vs 85.5% (p=0.004).

sections.title: Summary of Safety Results
sections.contentHtml: Grade ≥3 TEAEs: 18.6% (Arm A) vs 22.9% (Arm B). Grade ≥3 drug-induced hepatotoxicity: 8.3% vs 11.3%. QTcF >500 ms: 2.1% vs 0.6%. Peripheral neuropathy (any grade): 7.1% vs 8.1%. Tendinopathy / tendon rupture: 0.9% vs 0% (consistent with the known fluoroquinolone class effect). Nine deaths (4 Arm A, 5 Arm B); none adjudicated as drug-related.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.contentHtml: The 9-month levofloxacin-based regimen demonstrated non-inferiority to the standard 12-month WHO regimen for treatment success in rifampicin-sensitive spinal TB, with a comparable safety profile and superior treatment completion rates. These results support shortening of the standard duration of therapy for spinal TB in the NTEP and WHO guidelines, pending regulatory review.

sections.title: Protocol Signature Page
sections.contentHtml: Protocol SPINE-TB-2, Version 2.0, dated 18 June 2024. This signature page is executed by the sponsor's responsible medical officer, the coordinating principal investigator, and the biostatistician. Site principal investigators sign a local signature page at each centre before enrolling the first participant, confirming adherence to this protocol, ICH E6(R3) GCP, the Indian NDCT Rules 2019 (for Indian sites), and all applicable local regulations.

sections.title: Protocol Synopsis
sections.contentHtml:
SPINE-TB-2 is a Phase 3, open-label, randomised, multicentre, non-inferiority trial comparing a 9-month levofloxacin-based regimen with the WHO-standard 12-month regimen (2HRZE/10HRE) for rifampicin-sensitive spinal (Pott's) tuberculosis. 672 adult and adolescent participants will be randomised 1:1 across 24 sites in India, South Africa, the Philippines, and Brazil.

The primary endpoint is treatment success at 12 months post-therapy, defined per CDSCO composite criteria. The non-inferiority margin is 8 percentage points.

sections.title: Study Schema
sections.contentHtml: Study Schema: Screening (up to 14 days) → Randomisation (1:1, stratified by site, Pott's paraplegia, HIV status) → Treatment (9 or 12 months) → Post-therapy follow-up at Months 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, and 24. Monthly on-treatment visits (clinical, LFT, ECG, adherence). Sputum microbiology at Months 2, 4. MRI spine at baseline, Month 9, Month 18.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.contentHtml:
Spinal tuberculosis (Pott's disease) is the commonest form of musculoskeletal TB and remains a major cause of disability in TB-endemic settings. India accounts for the largest absolute burden globally. Historical regimens for spinal TB (including the MRC 1998 Working Party on Tuberculosis of the Spine) used 6- or 9-month durations, but WHO currently recommends 12 months, extrapolated from pulmonary TB evidence despite limited direct comparative data in the spinal form.

Shorter regimens would reduce patient and programme burden, improve adherence (currently ~75–85% at 12 months in programmatic conditions), and reduce cumulative drug toxicity. Levofloxacin has excellent bone penetration (bone:plasma ratio 0.6–1.3), demonstrated efficacy in drug-resistant TB regimens, and a favourable safety profile at the proposed 750 mg daily dose.

sections.title: Study Objectives (Primary + Secondary)
sections.contentHtml:
Primary objective. To demonstrate non-inferiority (margin 8 pp) of a 9-month levofloxacin-based regimen versus the WHO-standard 12-month regimen for treatment success at 12 months post-therapy.

Secondary objectives. (i) Culture conversion at Month 2 and Month 4; (ii) time to pain-free weight bearing; (iii) radiological healing per Bhojraj grading at Months 9 and 18; (iv) treatment completion rates; (v) 24-month relapse rate; (vi) safety and tolerability, with pre-specified attention to hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation, peripheral neuropathy, optic neuritis, and tendinopathy.

sections.title: Background (Spinal TB Epidemiology + MRC Trials Rationale)
sections.contentHtml:
Spinal TB accounts for ~1–3% of all TB cases globally and ~50% of musculoskeletal TB. Diagnosis typically relies on a composite of back pain >3 weeks, constitutional symptoms, radiological findings (vertebral destruction, paravertebral abscess, disc-space narrowing), and microbiological or histopathological confirmation where feasible.

The MRC Working Party on Tuberculosis of the Spine (Pattison, Darbyshire, et al., 1998–1999) randomised participants in India and Korea to 6-month versus 9-month regimens and found comparable outcomes at 10 years, supporting shorter durations historically. However, those trials predated widespread use of standardised short-course chemotherapy and were underpowered by modern standards. The SPINE-TB-2 trial provides contemporary randomised evidence of a 9-month regimen incorporating levofloxacin.

sections.title: Investigational Regimens (Levofloxacin FDC)
sections.contentHtml: The experimental regimen is a weight-banded fixed-dose combination (FDC) of levofloxacin + isoniazid + rifampicin + pyrazinamide (intensive phase, 2 months) and levofloxacin + isoniazid + rifampicin (continuation phase, 7 months). Levofloxacin dose: 750 mg daily (adults ≥50 kg); 500 mg daily (30–49 kg). FDCs are manufactured by Macleods Pharmaceuticals under WHO prequalification standards and supplied through the sponsor's central depot.

sections.title: Study Design (Randomised Non-Inferiority)
sections.contentHtml:
Open-label, randomised, parallel-group, non-inferiority trial. Participants are randomised 1:1 via a centralised web-based IVRS with permuted blocks stratified by (i) site, (ii) Pott's paraplegia at baseline (present vs absent), and (iii) HIV status (positive vs negative).

Although participants and investigators are unblinded (regimen durations differ), outcome assessors (microbiologists, independent MRI readers performing Bhojraj grading, and the endpoint adjudication committee) are blinded. The primary endpoint is adjudicated centrally.

sections.title: Subject Selection (Inclusion/Exclusion)
sections.contentHtml:
Inclusion. Age ≥14 years; newly diagnosed, previously untreated spinal TB with microbiological or composite diagnostic confirmation; rifampicin sensitivity confirmed; ability to attend scheduled follow-up for 24 months; informed consent (participant ± legal representative for minors).

Exclusion. MDR-TB or RR-TB; concurrent pulmonary cavitary disease requiring different treatment; pregnancy or breastfeeding at screening; ALT or AST >3×ULN at baseline; QTcF >450 ms (men) or >470 ms (women); known hypersensitivity to any component; severe liver cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B/C); concurrent participation in another investigational drug trial.

sections.title: Registration Procedures
sections.contentHtml: After informed consent, screening evaluations are completed within 14 days. Eligible participants are registered via IVRS; a unique participant identifier is assigned. Randomisation occurs at Visit 2 (Day 1) once all eligibility is confirmed and the participant is ready to start therapy.

sections.title: Treatment Plan (9-month vs 12-month)
sections.contentHtml:
Arm A (9-month regimen): 2 months of levofloxacin + isoniazid + rifampicin + pyrazinamide (FDC), followed by 7 months of levofloxacin + isoniazid + rifampicin (FDC). Doses weight-banded per NTEP conventions.

Arm B (12-month standard): 2 months of isoniazid + rifampicin + pyrazinamide + ethambutol (HRZE FDC), followed by 10 months of isoniazid + rifampicin + ethambutol (HRE FDC). This mirrors the WHO 2022 and NTEP 2023 recommended regimens for spinal TB.

All participants receive pyridoxine 25 mg daily and are counselled on alcohol avoidance.

sections.title: Dose Modifications for Hepatotoxicity
sections.contentHtml: Monthly LFTs are mandatory. Dose modification rules for hepatotoxicity: (i) ALT or AST 3–5×ULN without symptoms — continue therapy with weekly LFT monitoring; (ii) ALT or AST >5×ULN OR >3×ULN with symptoms (nausea, jaundice, RUQ pain) — interrupt ALL anti-TB drugs; investigate alternative aetiologies; (iii) upon normalisation (ALT <2×ULN), reintroduce one drug at a time following the ATS/BTS stepwise reintroduction protocol. Permanent discontinuation of the implicated drug is required for recurrent hepatotoxicity on rechallenge. SAE-0018 (DOC-105) illustrates application of these rules.

sections.title: Adverse Event Reporting
sections.contentHtml:
All AEs are recorded from first dose through the Month 24 visit, coded to MedDRA v27.0, and graded per CTCAE v5.0. SAEs are reported to the sponsor's pharmacovigilance within 24 hours of site awareness, and to CDSCO (and other regulators as applicable) per NDCT Rules 2019 timelines: suspected unexpected serious adverse reactions within 7 days (fatal/life-threatening) or 14 days (other).

AESIs: hepatotoxicity (any Grade ≥3); QT prolongation (QTcF >500 ms); tendinopathy or tendon rupture; peripheral neuropathy (any Grade ≥2); optic neuritis.

sections.title: Pharmaceutical Information
sections.contentHtml:
Levofloxacin is supplied as a WHO-prequalified FDC tablet manufactured by Macleods Pharmaceuticals, India. The standard regimen uses NTEP-supplied FDC tablets. Storage: ambient (not exceeding 30 °C), protected from humidity. Shelf life: 24 months from manufacture.

Drug accountability is maintained at every site using NTEP-compatible dispensing registers. Adherence is monitored via pill counts, 99DOTS/MERM where available, and monthly participant interviews.

sections.title: Study Calendar (Monthly LFT + Sputum)
sections.contentHtml: Study calendar includes monthly on-treatment visits (clinical exam, LFT, ECG, FBC, adherence review) through end of treatment; sputum microscopy and culture at Months 2 and 4; MRI spine at baseline, Month 9, Month 18; ophthalmology review at baseline and every 6 months. Post-therapy follow-up at Months 3, 6, 9, 12 (primary endpoint), 18, and 24 (relapse endpoint).

sections.title: Measurement of Effect (Culture Conversion + Bhojraj Grading)
sections.contentHtml:
The primary efficacy endpoint is composite treatment success at 12 months post-therapy, requiring: (a) no culture-positive relapse during post-therapy follow-up; (b) no radiological progression on Bhojraj grading; (c) no need for salvage anti-TB therapy; (d) alive and not died of TB.

Bhojraj grading (I = minimal; II = moderate; III = good healing; IV = complete healing) is performed by an independent radiology committee of 3 blinded readers using baseline, Month 9, and Month 18 MRI; discrepancies resolved by consensus.

sections.title: Statistical Considerations
sections.contentHtml:
Sample size calculation assumes a control-arm treatment success rate of 85%, true difference between arms of 0%, non-inferiority margin of 8 percentage points, one-sided alpha of 0.025, power of 85%, and a 10% loss-to-follow-up. The resulting target is 336 participants per arm (672 total).

Analysis: Miettinen-Nurminen 95% CI around the adjusted risk difference, with non-inferiority declared if the upper 95% CI bound is <+8 pp. Analyses are performed on the mITT and PP populations; concordance between the two populations is required for a positive non-inferiority conclusion. Pre-specified subgroup analyses: HIV status, Pott's paraplegia at baseline, country, diabetes, age (<18 vs ≥18).

sections.title: Multicentre Coordination (IN/ZA/PH/BR sites)
sections.contentHtml: The study is managed from AIIMS New Delhi (coordinating centre) with regional hubs at the University of Cape Town, PGH Manila, and FIOCRUZ (Rio de Janeiro). Data management is centralised in RedCap hosted by AIIMS, with monthly QC exports and quarterly site monitoring visits. The Clinical Trials Registry of India (CTRI/2023/06/054218) hosts the public registration.

sections.title: Publication Plan
sections.contentHtml: Primary results will be published in a peer-reviewed journal within 12 months of the primary endpoint analysis. Site principal investigators who meet ICMJE authorship criteria will be listed. Patient-level de-identified data will be made available via the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) 6 months after primary publication, under a controlled-access arrangement.

sections.title: Executive Summary
sections.contentHtml:
This is the second Development Safety Update Report (DSUR) for the SPINE-TB-2 investigational regimen, covering the DIBD anniversary period 15 July 2025 to 14 July 2026. The reporting period includes completion of enrolment (684 participants randomised through 28 February 2025) and the full on-treatment follow-up for the majority of participants.

The cumulative safety experience is consistent with the known class profiles of levofloxacin and the companion first-line anti-TB drugs. The DSMB reviewed data at scheduled meetings in October 2025 and April 2026 and recommended continuation without modification. No new safety signals were identified. The sponsor concludes that the benefit-risk profile of the 9-month investigational regimen remains favourable.
