sections.title: Introduction
sections.contentHtml: The investigational regimen under evaluation in SPINE-TB-2 is a 9-month levofloxacin-based FDC regimen (2 LfxHRZ / 7 LfxHR) for rifampicin-sensitive spinal tuberculosis. Levofloxacin is a well-established fluoroquinolone with WHO prequalification for TB indications. The Development International Birth Date (DIBD) is 15 July 2023 (first participant dosed in SPINE-TB-2). This Year 2 DSUR covers 15 July 2025 through 14 July 2026 and is prepared per ICH E2F.

sections.title: Worldwide Marketing Approval Status
sections.contentHtml: Levofloxacin has broad marketing authorisation globally (including India, EU, US, South Africa, Philippines, Brazil) for a range of bacterial infections and for drug-resistant TB regimens. The 9-month investigational combination is not approved as a specific indication; marketing authorisation for spinal TB will be pursued through CDSCO (India) and other regional regulators pending the primary endpoint analysis.

sections.title: Actions Taken in the Reporting Period for Safety Reasons
sections.contentHtml:
No safety-related regulatory actions, protocol modifications, or clinical holds occurred during the reporting period. The DSMB reviewed cumulative safety at two scheduled meetings (October 2025 and April 2026) and recommended continuation without modification on both occasions.

Protocol Amendment 1 (dated 10 December 2024) clarified operational handling of HIV co-infection and permitted enrolment of adolescents aged 14–17 following CDSCO consultation; neither change was triggered by a safety signal.

sections.title: Changes to Reference Safety Information
sections.contentHtml: No changes to the Reference Safety Information for the investigational regimen were made during the reporting period. The RSI remains Section 7 of the SPINE-TB-2 Investigator's Brochure, Edition 2 (dated 05 May 2024).

sections.title: Inventory of Clinical Trials (Ongoing + Completed)
sections.contentHtml: SPINE-TB-2 is the sole active sponsor-initiated trial of the investigational 9-month regimen. One investigator-initiated observational study (ongoing at NIRT Chennai) is tracking programmatic outcomes of a similar levofloxacin-based regimen in a non-randomised cohort and shares anonymised safety data with the sponsor on a quarterly basis.

sections.contentHtml:
During the reporting period, 68 serious adverse events (SAEs) were reported from SPINE-TB-2, of which 11 (16.2%) were classified as suspected unexpected serious adverse reactions (SUSARs) — principally cases of Grade 3 hepatotoxicity with unusual presentation (e.g. concurrent eosinophilia suggesting DRESS, 2 cases) and 1 case of tendon rupture (consistent with class but worthy of expedited reporting given rarity in the TB-FQ exposure window).

All SUSARs were reported to CDSCO within NDCT Rules 2019 timelines (7 days fatal/life-threatening; 14 days other). Line listings sorted by MedDRA SOC/PT and summary tabulations by arm are provided in Appendix A.

sections.title: Significant Findings from Clinical Trials
sections.contentHtml:
The most clinically significant finding during the reporting period was the completion of enrolment and the achievement of the primary endpoint milestone (last participant 12-month post-therapy visit on 30 June 2026). The topline primary analysis demonstrated non-inferiority of the 9-month regimen (see DOC-101 and DOC-102).

Safety during the reporting period remained consistent with the known profile. Grade ≥3 hepatotoxicity rates (Arm A 8.3%, Arm B 11.3%) were in line with historical TB-regimen hepatotoxicity rates. The QT-prolongation signal in Arm A (QTcF >500 ms in 2.1% vs 0.6%) is a known fluoroquinolone-class effect and did not translate to clinical arrhythmic events.

sections.title: Safety Findings from Non-interventional Studies
sections.contentHtml: The NIRT Chennai observational cohort (n=186) contributed real-world safety data confirming the trial findings: Grade ≥3 hepatotoxicity 9.1%; no QT-related SAE; two cases of Achilles tendinopathy that resolved with drug substitution.

sections.title: Other Clinical Trial / Study Safety Information
sections.contentHtml: No other sponsor-initiated clinical trial safety information falling outside the preceding sections is applicable for this reporting period. One compassionate-use authorisation (a single participant with HIV co-infection in a resource-limited setting) was granted under CDSCO Rule 101; no SAE occurred.

sections.title: Safety Findings from Marketing Experience
sections.contentHtml: Not applicable — the investigational 9-month regimen is not marketed as a specific indication. Levofloxacin itself has a well-characterised post-marketing safety profile summarised in the EU SmPC and US label; nothing in the reporting period alters that profile.

sections.title: Non-clinical Data
sections.contentHtml: No new non-clinical safety findings relevant to the investigational regimen were identified during the reporting period. Levofloxacin-related reproductive toxicology, juvenile toxicology, and chronic toxicity data have been reviewed and are summarised in the Investigator's Brochure Edition 2.

sections.title: Literature
sections.contentHtml: A targeted literature search (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane, 15 July 2025 to 14 July 2026) using “levofloxacin AND tuberculosis AND safety” identified 23 relevant publications. The most notable was a meta-analysis (Chen et al., Lancet Respir Med 2026) confirming the hepatotoxicity profile of fluoroquinolone-containing regimens is comparable to standard first-line therapy. No signal not already in the RSI emerged.

sections.title: Other DSURs
sections.contentHtml: No other DSURs for the investigational regimen are active. Levofloxacin PBRER/PSURs are managed by the respective marketing authorisation holders; these are not under GenBioCa's responsibility.

sections.title: Lack of Efficacy
sections.contentHtml: No efficacy failure concerns were identified during the reporting period. The DSMB did not activate the pre-specified futility stopping rule. The primary non-inferiority endpoint was met.

sections.title: Region-Specific Information
sections.contentHtml: Region-specific safety activities during the reporting period: (i) CDSCO periodic review submission (October 2025 and April 2026); (ii) a sponsor letter (14 January 2026) to all Indian site investigators reinforcing hepatotoxicity management per the ATS/BTS stepwise reintroduction protocol following the clustering of SAE-0018 (DOC-105) and 2 similar cases; (iii) SAHPRA correspondence on an isolated QT signal in a South African site (resolved; no action taken).

sections.title: Late-Breaking Information
sections.contentHtml: Between the data cutoff (14 July 2026) and DSUR submission (planned 15 October 2026), one additional Grade 3 hepatotoxicity event was reported from AIIMS Delhi (post-treatment); the event resolved with supportive care. No change to overall conclusions.

sections.title: Overall Safety Assessment (Hepatotoxicity + QT focus)
sections.contentHtml: Overall assessment: the 9-month levofloxacin-based regimen exhibited a safety profile consistent with the known profiles of its components. Hepatotoxicity (the dominant class-shared risk) occurred at rates comparable to the standard regimen (and numerically lower in Arm A, 8.3% vs 11.3%). QT prolongation (the FQ-specific signal) occurred as expected; clinical consequences were nil. No cardiovascular deaths occurred. The pre-specified hepatotoxicity and QT monitoring algorithm proved sufficient to prevent clinical harm.

sections.title: Summary of Important Risks
sections.contentHtml: Important identified risks: hepatotoxicity (shared across all first-line anti-TB drugs); QT prolongation (fluoroquinolone-specific); tendinopathy and tendon rupture (fluoroquinolone-specific); peripheral neuropathy (isoniazid-mediated, mitigated by pyridoxine); optic neuritis (ethambutol-specific in control arm); gastrointestinal intolerance; cutaneous reactions. Important potential risks: C. difficile infection; dysglycaemia (fluoroquinolone-related); photosensitivity. Missing information: safety in pregnancy, in paediatric patients <14 years, and in participants with Child-Pugh B/C cirrhosis.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.contentHtml: The benefit-risk profile of the 9-month levofloxacin-based investigational regimen remains favourable. No safety signal warranting modification of the Reference Safety Information or protocol was identified. The sponsor will continue post-treatment safety surveillance through the Month 24 relapse endpoint and submit the next DSUR by 31 October 2027.

sections.title: Patient Narrative (chronological prose)
sections.contentHtml:
Participant 002-0018 is a 46-year-old male (BMI 19.4) from a semi-urban district in Haryana, India, with newly diagnosed thoracic spinal tuberculosis (T9–T10 vertebral involvement, Xpert MTB/RIF positive, rifampicin-sensitive). Baseline co-morbidities: non-alcoholic (TTM negative), no viral hepatitis (HBsAg, anti-HCV negative), HIV negative, diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 7.1%, on metformin), occupational exposure to agricultural pesticides. Baseline ALT 32 U/L, AST 28 U/L, total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL.

He was randomised to Arm A on 05 September 2024 and started 2-month intensive-phase FDC (levofloxacin + isoniazid + rifampicin + pyrazinamide). Month 1 LFT (04 October 2024): ALT 68 U/L, AST 54 U/L — no action (within protocol limits). Month 2 LFT (02 November 2024): ALT 112 U/L (2.8×ULN), AST 94 U/L, total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL — weekly monitoring instituted per protocol.

On 22 November 2024 (Day 79), the participant presented to the clinic with 5 days of worsening nausea, anorexia, jaundice, and dark urine. Repeat labs showed ALT 420 U/L (10.5×ULN), AST 352 U/L (8.8×ULN), total bilirubin 3.8 mg/dL (direct 2.6 mg/dL), ALP 285 U/L, INR 1.3. All anti-TB drugs were held immediately. Hepatitis A/B/C/E serologies and autoimmune panel (ANA, SMA, anti-LKM) were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed no biliary obstruction. The participant was admitted for supportive care, intravenous N-acetylcysteine, and daily LFT monitoring. By Day 7 of drug cessation, ALT had declined to 128 U/L and bilirubin to 1.9 mg/dL; by Day 14, ALT was 48 U/L and bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL.

Per the ATS/BTS stepwise reintroduction protocol, rifampicin was reintroduced first on 14 December 2024 at full dose with LFT at 72 hours and 7 days; no rebound was observed. Isoniazid was added on 21 December 2024, again without rebound. Levofloxacin was reintroduced on 28 December 2024. Pyrazinamide was NOT reintroduced given the strong temporal association and lack of safer alternatives; the regimen was continued without pyrazinamide for the remainder of the intensive phase (6 additional weeks). The participant completed continuation-phase therapy per protocol and achieved treatment success at the 12-month post-therapy visit.

sections.title: Causality Considerations
sections.contentHtml:
Alternative aetiologies were systematically excluded: viral hepatitis (A/B/C/E serologies negative, HIV negative); autoimmune hepatitis (ANA, SMA, anti-LKM negative); alcoholic hepatitis (reliable history negative); biliary obstruction (ultrasound negative); ischaemic hepatitis (no hypotensive episode); non-prescription hepatotoxins including traditional medicines (direct questioning, family confirmation, negative).

Temporal relationship: progressive ALT rise over Months 1–2 with symptomatic decompensation at Day 79, consistent with the known temporal pattern of pyrazinamide-induced hepatotoxicity (peak incidence weeks 4–12). Dechallenge: rapid, complete biochemical resolution upon drug cessation. Rechallenge: stepwise reintroduction of rifampicin, isoniazid, and levofloxacin without rebound — strongly supportive of pyrazinamide as the specific offender. Pyrazinamide was not formally rechallenged (clinically contraindicated).

Overall causality assessment: probable (RUCAM score 7) for the anti-TB regimen as a whole; pyrazinamide as the most likely specific offender. Event is expected per the current RSI. SUSAR status: not applicable.

sections.title: Purpose and Narrative Conventions
sections.contentHtml:
This compendium contains patient-level narratives for all serious adverse events (SAEs) reported during SPINE-TB-2, prepared in accordance with ICH E3 Section 14.3.3 and CDSCO narrative-reporting expectations under NDCT Rules 2019. Each narrative follows a standardised template: patient characteristics, pre-event course, event description, management, outcome, and causality assessment.

Conventions. Subject identifiers are site-sequential (SSS-NNNN). Dates are presented as DD MMM YYYY (treatment-start-relative days in parentheses). Severity is CTCAE v5.0. MedDRA coding is v27.0. Causality uses standard categories: certain / probable / possible / unlikely / unrelated. “Expectedness” is per RSI (IB Section 7, Edition 2).

sections.title: Narrative 1 — Grade 3 Hepatotoxicity
sections.contentHtml: Narrative 1 — Subject 002-0018 — Grade 3 drug-induced hepatitis. A 46-year-old male with thoracic spinal TB on 9-month levofloxacin-based FDC developed symptomatic Grade 3 hepatotoxicity at Day 79 (peak ALT 420 U/L, bilirubin 3.8 mg/dL). All anti-TB drugs were held; biochemistry normalised within 14 days. Stepwise reintroduction (rifampicin → isoniazid → levofloxacin) was uneventful; pyrazinamide was permanently excluded. The participant completed modified therapy and achieved treatment success at 12 months. Causality: probable; most likely offender pyrazinamide. Full narrative in DOC-105.

sections.title: Narrative 2 — QT Interval Prolongation
sections.contentHtml: Narrative 2 — Subject 004-0046 — Grade 3 QT prolongation. A 52-year-old male (CMC Vellore, Arm A, no cardiac history, baseline QTcF 418 ms) presented at Month 3 (Day 92) routine ECG with QTcF 522 ms. He was asymptomatic. Electrolytes were within normal limits except mild hypomagnesaemia (1.5 mg/dL). Concomitant medications: ondansetron (started 5 days prior for nausea) — discontinued. Levofloxacin was held for 2 weeks; repeat ECG at 7 days post-hold showed QTcF 458 ms. Levofloxacin was resumed at 500 mg daily (dose-reduced from 750 mg) with weekly ECG; subsequent QTcF values remained <470 ms. The participant completed therapy without recurrence or arrhythmic events. Causality: probable (levofloxacin, with ondansetron as a contributing factor). Expected per RSI.

sections.title: Narrative 3 — Peripheral Neuropathy
sections.contentHtml: Narrative 3 — Subject 001-0092 — Grade 3 peripheral sensory neuropathy. A 61-year-old female (AIIMS Delhi, Arm B, baseline diabetes mellitus with HbA1c 8.2%, no baseline neuropathy) developed progressive bilateral stocking-pattern paraesthesia from Month 4, worsening to burning dysaesthesia by Month 6 and interfering with sleep (Grade 3). Nerve conduction studies at Month 7 showed axonal sensory polyneuropathy. Pyridoxine was increased from 25 mg to 100 mg daily. Isoniazid was initially continued at the standard dose; symptoms stabilised but did not resolve. On completion of therapy (Month 12), the participant reported partial improvement but residual Grade 2 sensory symptoms persisted. Causality: probable (isoniazid, with diabetes as a contributing factor). Expected per RSI. Outcome at 24 months: resolving but incomplete.

sections.title: Narrative 4 — Optic Neuritis
sections.contentHtml: Narrative 4 — Subject 006-0127 — Grade 3 optic neuritis. A 34-year-old male (KEM Mumbai, Arm B, no baseline visual symptoms, screening ophthalmology normal) reported progressive decrease in colour vision and central scotoma over 2 weeks starting Month 5 (Day 152). Visual acuity dropped from 20/20 to 20/80 bilaterally; red-green discrimination impaired. Fundoscopy showed bilateral optic disc pallor; MRI brain was unremarkable. Ophthalmology diagnosed ethambutol-related optic neuritis. Ethambutol was permanently discontinued; the regimen was continued with HRE → HR (ethambutol-free) for the continuation phase. Visual acuity recovered to 20/25 bilaterally by Month 10 and 20/20 by Month 18. Causality: probable (ethambutol). Expected per RSI. Outcome: resolved.

sections.title: Narrative 5 — Pregnancy Exposure
sections.contentHtml: Narrative 5 — Subject 003-0184 — Pregnancy during trial. A 28-year-old female (CMC Vellore, Arm A) with lumbar spinal TB conceived at Month 5 of therapy despite contraceptive counselling at enrolment (reported method failure). Pregnancy was detected at Month 6 (Day 182, estimated gestational age 7 weeks). After obstetric consultation and informed re-consent, levofloxacin was discontinued (potential foetal cartilage concerns); the regimen was continued with HRZ for the remaining intensive phase and HRE for continuation. Pregnancy proceeded uneventfully; a healthy female infant was delivered at 39 weeks (birth weight 2.9 kg). Infant development at 12 months post-delivery was normal (Denver screening test). Maternal spinal TB achieved treatment success. Causality assessment for pregnancy: not applicable (adverse event classification per ICH E2A pregnancy reporting). Outcome: live birth, no anomalies.

sections.title: Narrative 6 — Death (Non-treatment-related)
sections.contentHtml: Narrative 6 — Subject 011-0211 — Death (unrelated). A 54-year-old male (Lung Center of the Philippines, Arm B) with cervical spinal TB died on Day 198 (Month 6.5) in a road traffic accident while riding a motorcycle. Hospital records (reviewed by the sponsor's medical monitor) documented traumatic brain injury as the immediate cause of death. The participant had been clinically stable on study treatment at the last clinic visit 11 days prior; LFTs and ECG were within normal limits. Causality: unrelated to study treatment or underlying disease. The event was reported to the sponsor within 24 hours and to CDSCO/FDA Philippines within 7 days per NDCT Rules 2019 / local requirements. Outcome: fatal.

sections.title: Overview and Key Information
sections.contentHtml:
You are being asked to join a research study about the treatment of tuberculosis (TB) of the spine. This paper explains what the study is about. Please read it slowly. If you cannot read, someone will read it to you. You can ask questions at any time. Only sign if you understand and want to join.

Important things to know:

  • Taking part is your choice. Nobody can make you join.
  • If you say no, your TB treatment will still be given to you free of cost at your usual clinic.
  • You can stop the study at any time without losing any rights or care.
  • This study is about treatment duration — 9 months versus 12 months. The medicines are known medicines approved for TB.

sections.title: Why is this study being done?
sections.contentHtml:
We are doing this study to find out if a 9-month TB treatment works as well as the usual 12-month TB treatment for spinal TB. If 9 months is just as good as 12 months, it would mean a shorter treatment, fewer pills, and lower chance of side effects. It could also help many other people with spinal TB in the future.

The 9-month treatment uses a medicine called levofloxacin along with the usual TB medicines. Levofloxacin is already a known medicine used for other kinds of TB.

sections.title: What is the usual approach to spinal TB treatment?
sections.contentHtml: The usual treatment for spinal TB in India (and recommended by the World Health Organization) is 12 months of TB medicines: 2 months of 4 medicines, then 10 months of 3 medicines. This is given through the government TB programme (NTEP). The treatment usually works well, but it is long, and some people stop taking the medicines early, which can lead to the TB coming back or becoming harder to treat.

sections.title: What are my choices if I decide not to take part?
sections.contentHtml: If you do not want to join this study, you can still get full TB treatment free of cost at your usual NTEP centre, following the standard 12-month plan. Your TB doctor will care for you the same way as before. Not joining the study will not change your care in any way.

sections.title: What will happen if I decide to take part?
sections.contentHtml:
If you join:

  • We will first do tests (medical history, physical exam, blood tests, X-rays or MRI of your spine, HIV test, pregnancy test if applicable) to make sure the study is right for you. These take about 1–2 weeks.
  • You will be put into one of two groups by chance (like a coin toss). You will know which group you are in because the pill counts and duration are different.
  • You will visit the clinic every month for the first 9 or 12 months to collect your medicines and have check-ups.
  • After you finish treatment, we will see you again at 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, and 24 months to make sure the TB does not come back.

sections.title: What are the risks and benefits?
sections.contentHtml:
Possible benefits. You will get free TB medicines, free spine MRI scans, and free monthly blood tests. If you are in the 9-month group, you may finish treatment sooner. The information from this study may help other people with spinal TB in the future.

Possible risks and side effects.

  • Common (more than 1 in 10 people): nausea, loss of appetite, mild rash, feeling tired, numbness/tingling in hands or feet.
  • Serious but less common (fewer than 1 in 20): liver problems (yellow eyes, dark urine, pain in belly), vision problems (blurry vision — especially with the usual regimen), tendon pain or rupture (especially Achilles tendon in the 9-month group), fast or irregular heartbeat.
  • Very rare (fewer than 1 in 100): severe allergic reaction, severe liver damage, severe skin reaction.

We will check your liver with a blood test every month and your heart with ECG every month to catch any problems early. If a serious problem is found, we will change your treatment to keep you safe.

sections.title: Can I stop later?
sections.contentHtml:
Yes. Taking part is completely voluntary. You can leave the study at any time, for any reason, without having to explain. If you leave, your TB treatment will be transferred to your local NTEP centre and continued free of charge. Your decision to leave will not affect any care, benefits, or legal rights you have.

Your study doctor may also stop your study treatment if they feel it is in your best interest (for example, if you have severe side effects or if you become pregnant).

sections.title: What are the study groups (9-month vs 12-month)?
sections.contentHtml:
There are two groups. You will be put in one by chance (1 in 2):

  • Group A (new, 9-month plan): 2 months of 4 medicines (levofloxacin + isoniazid + rifampicin + pyrazinamide) → 7 months of 3 medicines (levofloxacin + isoniazid + rifampicin). All as one combined pill daily.
  • Group B (standard, 12-month plan): 2 months of 4 medicines (isoniazid + rifampicin + pyrazinamide + ethambutol) → 10 months of 3 medicines (isoniazid + rifampicin + ethambutol). All as one combined pill daily.

sections.title: Exams, tests, and procedures (Monthly LFT, MRI)
sections.contentHtml:
Tests and exams during the study:

  • Medical history and physical exam at each visit
  • Monthly blood tests (liver, kidney, blood counts) — about 1 teaspoon of blood each time
  • Monthly ECG (heart tracing) — takes about 10 minutes, painless
  • Spine MRI at the start, at 9 months, and at 18 months
  • Sputum tests at 2 and 4 months (if you can bring up sputum)
  • Eye check at the start and every 6 months (especially important if you are in Group B)
  • Pregnancy test monthly if you can become pregnant

sections.title: What are my responsibilities?
sections.contentHtml:
If you join, you agree to:

  • Take your medicines every day as directed. If you miss a dose, tell the study team.
  • Come to all your monthly visits (we will remind you by phone or SMS 1–2 days before).
  • Tell us about any new health problems or any new medicines, injections, or herbal remedies you take.
  • Use effective contraception during the study and for 3 months after your last dose if you can become pregnant (or if your partner can). Levofloxacin may harm an unborn baby.
  • Not join any other research study while you are in this one.

sections.title: What are the costs?
sections.contentHtml:
You will not have to pay anything for your TB medicines, the study tests, or the spine MRI scans. The study will reimburse your reasonable travel costs (bus/auto fare, meals) up to the equivalent of INR 500 per visit, in line with ICMR guidance. If you work and lose a half-day's wages to attend a study visit, you can also claim a daily-wage reimbursement of INR 300.

You will not be paid separately for taking part. The ethics committee has approved these amounts to compensate you fairly without being an inducement to join.

sections.title: What if I am injured?
sections.contentHtml:
If you are injured because of taking part in this study (for example, a serious side effect from a study medicine), the sponsor (GenBioCa India Pvt. Ltd.) will pay for the medical care you need to treat the injury, in line with Rules 39 and 40 of the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules 2019 (India). Compensation for study-related injury or study-related death is also provided per these Rules.

If you think you have been injured because of the study, call your study doctor right away: Prof. Priya Ramasubramaniam, AIIMS New Delhi, +91-11-2658-xxxx (24-hour emergency number). You do not give up any legal rights by signing this form.

sections.title: Who will see my medical information?
sections.contentHtml:
Your health records will be seen by the study team, the sponsor (GenBioCa), government regulators (CDSCO in India; SAHPRA, FDA Philippines, or ANVISA as applicable for other sites), and your institution's ethics committee. We will protect your privacy by using a study code instead of your name on paperwork that leaves the clinic.

Your data is handled under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDPA) in India — this means your data will be used only for the purposes you consent to here, kept only for as long as needed, protected with reasonable security measures, and you have the right to see your data, correct errors, and (after the study is complete) ask for it to be deleted. Your de-identified data may be used for related future TB research or shared with the WHO data platform. The ethics committee at your site has approved these privacy terms.

sections.title: Optional biobanking (sputum, blood)
sections.contentHtml:
You can choose to join the following optional sub-studies by ticking the boxes below. Saying no does not affect your main study participation.

  • Sputum biobanking. We will store extra sputum samples at the ICMR National Institute for Research in Tuberculosis (NIRT, Chennai) for up to 15 years for future TB research. Yes ___ / No ___
  • Blood biobanking. We will store extra blood samples (about 2 teaspoons at 3 timepoints) for future research on TB and drug responses. Yes ___ / No ___

Your samples will be de-identified and stored under DPDPA-compliant conditions. You can withdraw your biobanked samples at any time by writing to the study team.
